title: Is a point equally far from X and Y on the bisector?
description: A point P is the same distance from X and from Y. Triangles with the point B of the perpendicular bisector show that the line P B is itself the perpendicular bisector, so P lies on it. Keeko's doubt, that P can only be the middle point O, is broken by moving P along the line.
teaching_notes: One idea: pair P with a point of the bisector, use the earlier chain of congruent triangles, and use that a segment has only one perpendicular bisector. Watch for students who think an equidistant point must be the midpoint.

source: A point P is the same distance from X and Y, that is, PX = P
video_script.why: The child has seen that points on the perpendicular bisector are equally far from X and Y, but has not shown the other way round.
video_script.substitution: Pair P with the point B of the perpendicular bisector, repeat the two congruences from the last proof, and then use that a segment has one perpendicular bisector only.
video_script.anchor: A point P with PX = PY, and the perpendicular bisector AB of XY with the point B on it.
video_script.wrong_answer: P must be the middle point O
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks a point the same distance from X and Y can only be the middle point O of X Y, so P high above the segment could not qualify.
video_script.payoff_line: P lies on the line eigh B, the perpendicular bisector of X Y

final_answer.value: P lies on AB, the perpendicular bisector of XY
final_answer.spoken: P lies on the line eigh B, the perpendicular bisector of X Y

never_show: the word lies before the answer line
maths_rules: Given PX = PY. B is a point of the perpendicular bisector AB of XY, so BX = BY.
In triangles PBX and PBY: PX = PY, BX = BY, PB common, so triangle PBX is congruent to triangle PBY by SSS.
So angle XPB = angle YPB. If PB meets XY at O, triangles POX and POY: PX = PY, equal angles at P, PO common, so congruent by SAS.
So OX = OY and angle POX = angle POY = 90 degrees, so PB is a perpendicular bisector of XY.
A segment has only one perpendicular bisector, so line PB is the line AB, and P lies on AB.
video_script.design: One idea: the earlier chain of congruences, run with P in place of A. The last step uses that a segment has only one perpendicular bisector. Keeko's doubt is that an equidistant point must be the midpoint.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, join P to B. Look at triangles P B X and P B Y.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>P X equals P Y, and B X equals B Y.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The side P B is common. By side side side, the triangles are congruent.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>Let P B meet X Y at O.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, look at the small triangles P O X and P O Y.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two sides are equal, the angles between them are equal, and P O is common. By side angle side, they are congruent.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Then O X equals O Y, and each angle at O is a right angle.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: the line PB is a perpendicular bisector of XY; XY has only one perpendicular bisector, which is AB; so the line PB is the line AB

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, the line P B cuts X Y in half at a right angle.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But a segment has only one perpendicular bisector, and that is the line eigh B.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>This means the line P B and the line eigh B are the same line.

beats.on_screen: Answer: P lies on AB, the perpendicular bisector of XY
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>P lies on the line eigh B, the perpendicular bisector of X Y.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Every point equidistant from X and Y lies on that line.
